name: Sustained 700 C (pottery kiln)
note: Already available wherever there is an updraught pottery kiln, wood fired. Free starting capability. Glazes, bricks, lime, glass working.

name: Sustained 1100 C (hand-blown charcoal)
note: Already reached wherever bloomery iron, bronze casting and glass melting are practised. A man on a bellows tops out near here. Everything above this rung needs a machine.

name: Sustained 1300 C (water-blown continuous blast)
note: Liquid cast iron lives here. The jump from 1100 to 1300 is not more fuel, it is more AIR, continuously. This single rung is the difference between a bloomery civilisation and a foundry civilisation.

diagnosis_instrument.needed_words: a furnace temperature known to within 50 degrees

name: Sustained 1600 C (regenerative preheat)
note: Siemens regenerative preheat recycles flue heat into the incoming air. Crucible steel, open hearth, porcelain. You cannot get here by burning more charcoal; you must recycle the heat you are already throwing away.

name: 2000 C localised (oxy-hydrogen blowpipe)
note: An oxy-hydrogen blowpipe is a jet of hydrogen burning in pure oxygen. Without the nitrogen of air to soak up heat, the flame is far hotter than any furnace of the time, but it heats only a small spot, so it works on small objects only. It needs both gases made, stored and fed to the nozzle separately, because mixed gas can explode back into the supply. This heat can melt platinum, work fused quartz and make lime glow.

diagnosis_instrument.needed_words: a flame temperature known to within 50 degrees

name: 3000 C+ (electric arc / resistance)
note: Temperatures above any fuel flame, reached by passing a heavy electric current through a gap (an arc) or through a resistant conductor so that it glows. It needs a large steady supply of electric power and electrodes that survive the heat. No chemical flame reaches this hot, so it is the only route to calcium carbide, ferroalloys, tungsten, artificial graphite and synthetic corundum (a hard crystalline aluminium oxide).

name: Tolerance 1 mm (skilled hand craft)
note: Already reached, and reached well, by any tradition with serious carpentry, masonry and bronze casting (the Antikythera gearwork is the standing proof). Free.

name: Tolerance 0.1 mm (file, scraper, gauge)
note: The ability to make and check parts to a tenth of a millimetre by hand tools. It works by scraping and filing a surface against a reference plane, then checking it with a gauge, so the part is only as good as the reference. Without a true reference plane and a gauge the founder cannot tell good work from bad. It opens clock wheels, lock work and screw threads that actually fit.

name: Tolerance 0.01 mm (slide rest, lead screw, micrometer)
note: Take the tool out of the operator's hand and accuracy stops depending on his wrist. Steam pistons, interchangeable parts, precision instruments.

name: Tolerance 1 micron (lapping, grinding, optical flats)
note: Lapping with loose abrasive plus interference fringes to check. Gauge blocks, ball bearings, lens moulds, injector nozzles.

name: Tolerance 0.1 micron (interferometric)
note: Making and checking surfaces to a fraction of the wavelength of light. Flatness and spacing are read from interference fringes, the light and dark bands produced when two reflected light beams meet, so the measuring tool is light itself. It needs the finest lapped optical flats and a way to count fringes. It underlies precision optical surfaces, diffraction gratings and, much later, semiconductor lithography.

name: Rough vacuum, about 1 torr (piston pump)
note: A rough vacuum is made with a piston pump, a cylinder where a sealed piston draws air out through valves. Leather around the piston makes the seal, and each stroke removes part of the air that is left. Leaks past the leather and the space left at the end of each stroke stop it going lower. It is enough to show that air has weight and pressure, and for barometers and condensers, but it leaves too much gas for any electron device.

name: High vacuum, about 1e-3 torr (Sprengel mercury drop)
note: THE cheap shortcut. Falling mercury drops each trap a slug of gas and carry it out. No pistons, no seals, no tolerances. Incandescent lamps and discharge tubes live here.

name: Very high vacuum, 1e-6 torr (diffusion pump plus getters)
note: A vacuum a thousand times better than a mercury drop pump gives, reached with a diffusion pump (a fast jet of hot vapour that sweeps stray gas out) and getters (chemicals that absorb the last gas). The diffusion pump cannot start against open air, so a motor-driven backing pump is needed to rough the chamber first. Joints must be machined tight enough not to leak. It makes vacuum tubes, X-ray tubes and evaporated coatings possible.

name: Ultra high vacuum, 1e-9 torr (bakeable metal systems)
note: A vacuum so empty that a surface stays clean for hours. Rubber and grease seals give off gas, so the system is built of metal with crushable metal gaskets and is baked hot to drive trapped gas out of its walls, then pumped by ion pumps (which bury gas molecules in a metal surface). It needs stainless steel and very fine machining. It opens surface science and semiconductor processing.

name: Purity 99% (careful classical refining)
note: Cupellation, fire refining, recrystallisation. Any advanced ancient metallurgical tradition nearly reaches this for silver and gold already.

name: Purity 99.99% (electrorefining, fractional crystallisation)
note: Chemically pure material, with no more than one part in ten thousand of impurity. It is reached by electrorefining (using electric current to move only the wanted metal from an impure bar onto a clean plate) and fractional crystallisation (repeated partial freezing, where impurities stay in the liquid). You cannot claim a purity you cannot measure, so this rung is gated on quantitative analysis as much as on process.

name: Purity 99.9999% (fractional distillation of volatile compounds)
note: Purify the COMPOUND, not the element. Germanium tetrachloride boils at 86 C and fractionates like brandy; germanium metal does not.

name: Purity 1 part in 1e9 (zone refining)
note: No chemistry reaches here. A travelling molten zone sweeps impurities to one end because most are more soluble in liquid than in solid. This one trick is what makes semiconductors possible at all.

name: Draught-animal muscle power
note: Oxen, horses, mules, or comparable domesticated draught animals can supply sustained traction and rotary power; an ox can provide roughly 400 W. This capability is not universal human muscle power and is absent where suitable working animals and harness traditions do not exist.

name: Water power, tens of kW on one shaft
note: Already available and barely used for anything but grinding grain, wherever a water wheel turns (Rome's Barbegal runs 16 overshot wheels and still mostly grinds grain). The technology gap is imagination, not engineering.

power_tier.label: water power, tens of kW on one shaft

name: Steam power, portable, hundreds of kW
note: Mechanical power from a steam engine that can be set up anywhere fuel and water can be carried, with no need for a river. It needs boilers strong enough to hold high pressure without bursting, which is the hard part. Until a site has no usable stream, water power is cheaper and needs a far shorter prerequisite chain, so the founder should go to steam only when location forces it.

power_tier.label: portable steam power, hundreds of kW

name: Local electric power, kW scale
note: A local supply of electricity, produced by turning a dynamo (a machine that makes current by spinning wire coils in a magnetic field) with a water wheel. One dynamo on the millpond shaft you already built is enough to power arc lights, electroplating and a laboratory. It is limited by what the one shaft can turn and by wires that must be made and insulated, and it serves only buildings near the mill.

name: Grid electric power, MW scale
note: The precondition for every energy-intensive process: arc furnaces, electrolysis, aluminium, and the sustained laboratory power a purity programme eats.

power_tier.label: grid electric power, MW scale (central generation)

name: Reproducible length standard
note: A length standard that anyone can reproduce and that outlives its maker. The founder has master bars cast in bronze, in triplicate, and keeps them in three cities so that a loss or a forgery in one place can be checked against the others. Without this nothing you write down survives you, because every measurement in a recipe is a length that someone else must be able to match.

name: Mass to 1 milligram
note: Weighing to a thousandth of a gram. The balance has hard agate knife edges that carry the beam with almost no friction, and it sits in a closed case against draughts. It needs an analytical balance and carefully calibrated weights. It is the instrument that turns alchemy into chemistry, because it lets the founder show that matter is conserved in a reaction.

name: Temperature to a few degrees (liquid in glass)
note: Fixed points at melting ice and boiling water. Without a repeatable scale no thermal recipe can be transmitted to anyone not standing beside you.

name: High temperature (clay contraction and colour pyrometry)
note: Wedgwood-style contraction pyrometer plus a calibrated colour scale. You cannot control a furnace whose temperature you cannot read.

name: Time to the second (pendulum)
note: Keeping time to the second using a pendulum clock. A pendulum swings at a rate fixed by its length, so a clock regulated by one stays steady day after day, unlike water clocks and sundials. It needs a clock mechanism that gives the pendulum a small push each swing. It matters for navigation and physics, and later for every electrical measurement.

name: Time to the millisecond (chronograph, tuning fork)
note: Timing events to a thousandth of a second. A chronograph records short intervals mechanically, and a tuning fork supplies a steady vibration to count against, so the interval is read as a number of vibrations. It needs the second-accurate clock to calibrate against and parts made to fine tolerance. It serves ballistics, engine indicating (recording pressure through a stroke) and telegraphy.

name: Absolute electrical units
note: A coil of known geometry and the Earth's field give absolute current with no calibrated instrument to start from. This is how the electrical metrology bootstrap escapes its own circularity.

name: Interferometric length (wavelengths of light)
note: Measuring length against the wavelength of light, a physical constant, instead of against a bar of metal. Two beams of light from the same source are split and rejoined, and the pattern of bright and dark bands shows how far one path is longer than the other. It needs a spectroscope to know which light is used and optical flats to judge flatness. A bar can warp or be lost; a wavelength cannot.

name: Oxygen and hydrogen in quantity
note: Zinc or iron with acid gives hydrogen; heating manganese dioxide or a chlorate gives oxygen. Needed for the oxy-hydrogen torch, for fused quartz, for balloons, and later for reducing germanium oxide to metal. Hydrogen and air is an explosive mixture over a very wide range; be disciplined.
